FAMILY LAW FACILITATOR ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

DECLARATION -- SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Family Law Facilitator Act (Family Code sections 10000 through 10015), which requires each superior court to maintain an office of the family law facilitator to assist parties in a matter between Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan, case number CGC-26-123456, pending in Sacramento County. It describes the Legislature's stated purpose in creating the office, the office's required staffing, the categories of proceedings the statute reaches, the services the statute lists, the additional duties a superior court may add by local rule (including facilitator-conducted mediation of support-related issues and a domestic-violence-specific meeting protocol), the statute's no-cost-to-the-parties and hearing-access provisions, how the statute interacts with services provided by a local child support agency, and the statute's own limits on the facilitator's role, including that the facilitator does not represent any party and that no attorney-client relationship or privilege is created. It does not itself request or grant any facilitator appointment, service, mediation, or order, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about how the Family Law Facilitator Act applies to a specific case.

THE LEGISLATURE'S STATED FINDINGS AND PURPOSE
Under California law, the Legislature that enacted the Family Law Facilitator Act found that child and spousal support are serious legal obligations whose enforcement was frequently delayed by protracted custody and visitation litigation, and that family courts were unduly burdened with heavy caseloads and insufficient personnel. The Legislature further found a compelling state interest in a speedy, conflict-reducing, cost-effective system for resolving child support, spousal support, and health insurance issues that is accessible to families who cannot afford legal representation, and stated its intent to make services piloted in the Superior Courts of Santa Clara and San Mateo Counties available statewide.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Child and spousal support are serious legal obligations. The entry of a child support order is frequently delayed while parents engage in protracted litigation concerning custody and visitation. The current system for obtaining child and spousal support orders is suffering because the family courts are unduly burdened with heavy case loads and do not have sufficient personnel to meet increased demands on the courts."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10001(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Family Code section 10001, subdivision (a)(1) -- a legislative finding on support-order delay and court caseloads (a subdivision of the same Section 10001 as the next citation, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10001.)
  "There is a compelling state interest in having a speedy, conflict-reducing system for resolving issues of child support, spousal support, and health insurance that is cost-effective and accessible to families that cannot afford legal representation. (b) Therefore, it is the intent of the Legislature to make the services provided in the family law pilot projects in the Counties of Santa Clara and San Mateo available to unrepresented parties in the superior courts of all California counties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10001(a)(4)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), Family Code section 10001, subdivision (a)(4) and the adjoining statement of legislative intent in subdivision (b) -- also part of Section 10001, not an independent source from the previous citation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10001.)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Family Code section 10001 -- the first is finding (a)(1) and the second is finding (a)(4) together with the adjoining statement of intent in subdivision (b) -- so they are not independent sources of each other, only two excerpts of one legislative findings section. Legislative findings describe the Legislature's own stated rationale for enacting a statute; they are not themselves an operative rule of law, and a court is not bound to reach the same policy conclusions the findings recite. This clause also does not address findings (a)(2) and (a)(3), which describe the Santa Clara and San Mateo pilot-project reports and survey results underlying the Legislature's conclusion.

REQUIRED OFFICE, ATTORNEY STAFFING, AND APPOINTMENT
Under California law, each superior court is required to maintain an office of the family law facilitator, and that office must be staffed by an attorney licensed to practice law in California who has mediation or litigation experience, or both, in the field of family law. The family law facilitator is appointed by the superior court.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Each superior court shall maintain an office of the family law facilitator. The office of the family law facilitator shall be staffed by an attorney licensed to practice law in this state who has mediation or litigation experience, or both, in the field of family law. The family law facilitator shall be appointed by the superior court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10002 (California Legislative Information text), the office, staffing qualification, and appointment requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10002.)
  Known gap: The statute states a staffing qualification and an appointment mechanism, but does not itself specify the facilitator's term of appointment, removal process, caseload or minimum staffing levels, or funding source for the office beyond what is addressed elsewhere in this division; those details are left to each superior court's own administration and local rules, which this clause does not survey.

THE CATEGORIES OF PROCEEDINGS THIS DIVISION REACHES
Under California law, the Family Law Facilitator Act applies to actions or proceedings for temporary or permanent child support, spousal support, health insurance, child custody, or visitation arising in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, legal separation, or exclusive child custody, or arising under the Uniform Parentage Act or the Domestic Violence Prevention Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This division shall apply to all actions or proceedings for temporary or permanent child support, spousal support, health insurance, child custody, or visitation in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, legal separation, or exclusive child custody, or pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12) or the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200))."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10003 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory scope provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10003.)
  Known gap: This section defines the division's scope by reference to two other statutory schemes -- the Uniform Parentage Act (Family Code Part 3 of Division 12, commencing with Section 7600) and the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Family Code Division 10, commencing with Section 6200) -- without restating either scheme's own substantive rules, which this clause does not independently verify. It also does not address Section 10008's separate carve-out and re-inclusion for cases receiving local child support agency services under Section 17400, covered in a separate clause of this document, or reach family law matters outside the listed categories, such as pure property-division disputes.

THE NON-EXHAUSTIVE LIST OF CORE SERVICES
Under California law, the services a family law facilitator provides include, but are not limited to: providing educational materials to parents about the process of establishing parentage and establishing, modifying, and enforcing child support and spousal support in the courts; distributing necessary court forms and voluntary declarations of paternity; providing assistance in completing forms; preparing support schedules based on statutory guidelines; and providing referrals to the local child support agency, family court services, and other community agencies and resources serving parents and children. In counties where a family law information center exists, the facilitator must provide assistance on child support issues.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Services provided by the family law facilitator shall include, but are not limited to, the following: providing educational materials to parents concerning the process of establishing parentage and establishing, modifying, and enforcing child support and spousal support in the courts; distributing necessary court forms and voluntary declarations of paternity; providing assistance in completing forms; preparing support schedules based upon statutory guidelines; and providing referrals to the local child support agency, family court services, and other community agencies and resources that provide services for parents and children."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10004 (California Legislative Information text), the enumerated, non-exhaustive services provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10004.)
  Known gap: The statute's own "shall include, but are not limited to" language means this list is a floor rather than an exhaustive ceiling, so the services actually offered in a given county can exceed this list (or, where staff and funding are constrained, fall short of fully delivering it), and this clause does not survey any particular county's actual practice. It also does not address whether any of these services amount to legal advice; a related, separate provision of this division addresses the facilitator's no-representation limits.

ADDITIONAL DUTIES A COURT MAY ADD BY LOCAL RULE
Under California law, a superior court may, by local rule, designate additional duties for the family law facilitator beyond the core services statute. These optional duties can include meeting with litigants to mediate issues of child support, spousal support, and maintenance of health insurance -- with priority given to actions in which one or both parties are unrepresented -- drafting stipulations on issues the parties agree to, reviewing paperwork and preparing support schedules to advise the judge whether a matter is ready to proceed, assisting the clerk in maintaining records, preparing formal orders consistent with the court's announced order when both parties are unrepresented, and serving as a special master and making findings to the court, unless the facilitator already served as mediator in that same case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "By local rule, the superior court may designate additional duties of the family law facilitator, which may include, but are not limited to, the following: (1) Meeting with litigants to mediate issues of child support, spousal support, and maintenance of health insurance, subject to Section 10012. Actions in which one or both of the parties are unrepresented by counsel shall have priority."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10005(a) (California Legislative Information text), the local-rule additional-duties provision, subdivision (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10005.)
  "Serving as a special master in proceedings and making findings to the court unless the family law facilitator has served as a mediator in that case."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10005(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text), the special-master duty and its own-mediator disqualification, a further paragraph of the same subdivision (a) as the previous citation, not an independent source from it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10005.)
  Known gap: These duties are locally optional -- the statute says a court "may" designate them by local rule -- so whether a particular county's facilitator actually performs mediation, drafts stipulations, or serves as a special master depends on that county's own local rules, which this clause does not survey. The mediation duty is also expressly made subject to a separate domestic-violence meeting protocol addressed in another clause of this document, and this clause does not restate the statute's separate, resource-conditioned list of further discretionary duties (court research assistance and bar/community outreach programs) found in the same section's subdivision (b).

A DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE SAFEGUARD FOR FACILITATOR-CONDUCTED MEDIATION
Under California law, where a superior court has designated facilitator-conducted mediation of support and health-insurance issues as a local-rule duty, and there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties or a protective order is in effect, the facilitator must meet with the parties separately and at separate times if the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury, or the party protected by the order, requests it. Any intake form the facilitator's office requires before mediation begins must state that this separate-meeting option is available on request.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In a proceeding in which mediation is required pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 10005, where there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or protected by the order, the family law facilitator shall meet with the parties separately and at separate times."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10012(a) (California Legislative Information text), the separate-meeting requirement, subdivision (a) (a subdivision of the same Section 10012 as the next citation, not an independent source of it) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10012.)
  "Any intake form that the office of the family law facilitator requires the parties to complete before the commencement of mediation shall state that, if a party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or a party protected by a protective order so requests, the mediator will meet with the parties separately and at separate times."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10012(b) (California Legislative Information text), the intake-form disclosure requirement, subdivision (b) of the same Section 10012 as the previous citation, not an independent source of it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10012.)
  Known gap: This safeguard is tied specifically to the facilitator's own optional mediation duty under Section 10005, subdivision (a)(1); it is a separate mechanism from the mandatory custody-and-visitation mediation program under Family Code Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 3160), which has its own, independently verified domestic-violence procedures addressed elsewhere in this corpus. This clause does not address what happens if a facilitator's office lacks the staffing to hold genuinely separate sessions, which the statute does not itself resolve.

NO COST TO THE PARTIES, AND ULTIMATE ACCESS TO A HEARING
Under California law, the court must provide the family law facilitator to the parties at no cost, and the court must adopt a protocol under which all litigants -- whether represented by counsel or not -- retain ultimate access to a hearing before the court.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The court shall adopt a protocol wherein all litigants, both unrepresented by counsel and represented by counsel, have ultimate access to a hearing before the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10006 (California Legislative Information text), the hearing-access protocol requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10006.)
  "The court shall provide the family law facilitator at no cost to the parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10007 (California Legislative Information text), the no-cost requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10007.)
  Known gap: These two one-sentence requirements come from separate statutory sections (10006 and 10007) within the same division, so unlike some other clauses in this document they are independent of each other, but each is stated only at a high level: the statute does not specify what a court's hearing-access "protocol" must contain beyond guaranteeing that ultimate access, and "no cost" applies to the facilitator's own services -- it does not address court filing fees or other litigation costs, which are set by separate statutes and local court fee schedules this clause does not survey.

INTERACTION WITH LOCAL CHILD SUPPORT AGENCY (TITLE IV-D) CASES
Under California law, this division generally does not apply to a child for whom services are provided or required to be provided by a local child support agency under Family Code Section 17400. Where local child support agency services are being provided, either parent may still use the facilitator's core services listed in Section 10004, but a custodial parent receiving local child support agency services must obtain the agency's written authorization before using the facilitator's local-rule support-related services under Section 10005. The statute states that it is not intended to limit a local child support agency's own duties to seek child support or to limit or supersede other provisions of the code respecting temporary child support.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), nothing in this chapter shall be construed to apply to a child for whom services are provided or required to be provided by a local child support agency pursuant to Section 17400. (b) In cases in which the services of the local child support agency are provided pursuant to Section 17400, either parent may utilize the services of the family law facilitator that are specified in Section 10004. In order for a custodial parent who is receiving the services of the local child support agency pursuant to Section 17400 to utilize the services specified in Section 10005 relating to support, the custodial parent must obtain written authorization from the local child support agency."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10008 (California Legislative Information text), the Title IV-D interaction provision, subdivisions (a) and (b) together (both part of the same Section 10008, not independent of each other) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10008.)
  Known gap: This section describes the interaction between the two programs but does not itself state the procedure or standard a local child support agency uses to grant or deny the written authorization it requires, and it does not restate Section 17400's own scope, which this clause does not independently verify. It also singles out the "custodial parent" for the written-authorization requirement without addressing a noncustodial parent's access to Section 10005 services in a Section 17400 case.

NO REPRESENTATION, NO ATTORNEY-CLIENT RELATIONSHIP, NO PRIVILEGE
Under California law, the family law facilitator does not represent any party, and no attorney-client relationship is created between a party and the facilitator as a result of any information or services the facilitator provides. The facilitator must give conspicuous notice that no attorney-client relationship exists, and that notice must include the advice that the absence of an attorney-client relationship means communications between a party and the facilitator are not privileged, and that the facilitator may provide services to the other party as well.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The family law facilitator shall not represent any party. No attorney-client relationship is created between a party and the family law facilitator as a result of any information or services provided to the party by the family law facilitator. The family law facilitator shall give conspicuous notice that no attorney-client relationship exists between the facilitator, its staff, and the family law litigant. The notice shall include the advice that the absence of an attorney-client relationship means that communications between the party and the family law facilitator are not privileged and that the family law facilitator may provide services to the other party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 10013 (California Legislative Information text), the no-representation, no-attorney-client-relationship, and no-privilege provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=10013.)
  Known gap: The statute requires "conspicuous notice" of these limits but does not itself prescribe the notice's exact wording or format; a separate provision of this division (Section 10015, not independently verified in this document) directs the Judicial Council to create the forms that carry out this and related notice requirements. This clause also addresses only the attorney-client privilege; it does not address whether any other evidentiary privilege could apply to a facilitator communication.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT -- NOT A FACILITATOR APPOINTMENT OR COURT ORDER
I, Jordan Lee, and I, Pat Morgan, each acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's Family Law Facilitator Act in connection with case number CGC-26-123456 pending in Sacramento County.

Executed on September 1, 2026.

☐ _________________________ Jordan Lee, signature

☐ _________________________ Pat Morgan, signature

Oakland, California

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing or proceeding in the appropriate California superior court. It does not itself appoint, engage, or request the services of a family law facilitator, does not determine which local-rule duties the office of the family law facilitator performs in Sacramento County, and does not create any attorney-client relationship or privilege. Only the family law facilitator's office and the local rules applicable in Sacramento County determine what services are actually available in a specific case, and this is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

expectedJSON.body: Under California law, this division generally does not apply to a child for whom services are provided or required to be provided by a local child support agency under Family Code Section 17400. Where local child support agency services are being provided, either parent may still use the facilitator's core services listed in Section 10004, but a custodial parent receiving local child support agency services must obtain the agency's written authorization before using the facilitator's local-rule support-related services under Section 10005. The statute states that it is not intended to limit a local child support agency's own duties to seek child support or to limit or supersede other provisions of the code respecting temporary child support.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10008 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the Title IV-D interaction provision, subdivisions (a) and (b) together (both part of the same Section 10008, not independent of each other)
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), nothing in this chapter shall be construed to apply to a child for whom services are provided or required to be provided by a local child support agency pursuant to Section 17400. (b) In cases in which the services of the local child support agency are provided pursuant to Section 17400, either parent may utilize the services of the family law facilitator that are specified in Section 10004. In order for a custodial parent who is receiving the services of the local child support agency pursuant to Section 17400 to utilize the services specified in Section 10005 relating to support, the custodial parent must obtain written authorization from the local child support agency.

expectedJSON.gap: This section describes the interaction between the two programs but does not itself state the procedure or standard a local child support agency uses to grant or deny the written authorization it requires, and it does not restate Section 17400's own scope, which this clause does not independently verify. It also singles out the "custodial parent" for the written-authorization requirement without addressing a noncustodial parent's access to Section 10005 services in a Section 17400 case.

expectedJSON.body: Under California law, the family law facilitator does not represent any party, and no attorney-client relationship is created between a party and the facilitator as a result of any information or services the facilitator provides. The facilitator must give conspicuous notice that no attorney-client relationship exists, and that notice must include the advice that the absence of an attorney-client relationship means communications between a party and the facilitator are not privileged, and that the facilitator may provide services to the other party as well.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10013 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the no-representation, no-attorney-client-relationship, and no-privilege provision
citations.quote: The family law facilitator shall not represent any party. No attorney-client relationship is created between a party and the family law facilitator as a result of any information or services provided to the party by the family law facilitator. The family law facilitator shall give conspicuous notice that no attorney-client relationship exists between the facilitator, its staff, and the family law litigant. The notice shall include the advice that the absence of an attorney-client relationship means that communications between the party and the family law facilitator are not privileged and that the family law facilitator may provide services to the other party.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute requires "conspicuous notice" of these limits but does not itself prescribe the notice's exact wording or format; a separate provision of this division (Section 10015, not independently verified in this document) directs the Judicial Council to create the forms that carry out this and related notice requirements. This clause also addresses only the attorney-client privilege; it does not address whether any other evidentiary privilege could apply to a facilitator communication.
